pests.name: Squash vine borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A previously vigorous vine wilts suddenly in mid to late summer, often near the base, and you find sawdust-like frass oozing from a hole low on the main stem. Cutting the stem open reveals a fat white caterpillar tunneling inside. Whole plants can collapse once the borer severs the stem's water flow.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A healthy pumpkin plant wilts all at once in summer, and you see sawdust-like specks coming out of a hole near the base of the stem. Inside the stem is a fat white grub.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth, which lays eggs at the stem base in early summer. The hatching larvae bore into the main stem and feed inside for several weeks, cutting off the plant's water and collapsing the vine. There can be two generations in the South.
pests.cause_beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of the stem in early summer, and the grubs that hatch tunnel inside and kill the vine from within.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Once a borer is inside, slit the stem lengthwise with a knife, remove the larva, and bury that node under moist soil to re-root. Bury vines at the joints as they run so a damaged plant can survive on secondary roots. Removing and destroying infested vines reduces next year's brood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If you catch it early, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover that spot with damp soil so it can re-root. Pull and destroy badly damaged vines.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover from planting until flowering to exclude the egg-laying moths, then remove it for pollination. Plant early or time a planting after the main flight, scout the stem base for frass from early summer, and grow more tolerant cucurbits where pressure is severe. Till in late winter and rotate to disrupt overwintering pupae.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants with a light fabric row cover until they flower to keep the moths out, then take it off so bees can reach the flowers. Check the base of the stem for sawdust-like specks starting in early summer, and clean up old vines at the end of the season.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed vines wilt rapidly and turn brittle, a damage pattern sometimes called anasa wilt. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs on the undersides of leaves near the base of the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: The squash bug, a true bug that feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the vines. Populations build through the season and are hardest to control once nymphs are large; the bugs overwinter as adults in garden debris.
pests.cause_beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They breed through the summer and hide in plant debris over winter.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since large nymphs and adults are tough to kill.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover on young plants until flowering, clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, and rotate cucurbits. Scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season and act before nymphs mature.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower, check under the leaves for eggs early in the season, and clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter.

pests.name: Cucumber beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small yellow beetles, striped or spotted, chew young leaves, stems, and flowers, and can scar developing fruit. The bigger threat is indirect: striped and spotted cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt, so beetle feeding on seedlings can be followed weeks later by sudden, runaway vine wilt.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers, especially of young plants. Worse, they can spread a disease called bacterial wilt that makes the vines collapse later.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and carry the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt in their gut, infecting plants as they feed. Seedlings are most vulnerable; once pumpkin plants have four or more leaves they tolerate some feeding, and bacterial wilt is generally less severe in pumpkin and squash than in cucumber and melon.
pests.cause_beginner: Cucumber beetles feed on pumpkin plants and carry the germ that causes bacterial wilt, infecting the plant as they chew. Young seedlings are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover removed at flowering, hand-pick beetles, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce numbers. Where bacterial wilt is a known problem, controlling the beetles is the most effective control of the disease, since there is no cure once a plant is infected.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with row cover (remove it when flowers open), pick the beetles off, and use yellow sticky traps. Keeping the beetles down is the best way to avoid the wilt disease they spread.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the vulnerable stage, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers that vector wilt.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where squash-family crops grew last year.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects gather on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and turn yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up quickly on stressed or over-fertilized plants. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several aphid species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply fast, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave behind grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches appear first on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and sugars, and exposes pumpkins to sunscald.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they turn yellow and brown and die. The plant fades early, and the pumpkins may not size up well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi that thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is one of the most common late-season pumpkin diseases.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat at the first spots, before it spreads, with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves. Once it covers the plant it is hard to stop.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants generously for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign, since prevention and early action beat rescue.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants plenty of room so air moves between them, plant in full sun, and water at the base. Start checking in midsummer and act at the first white spots.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular yellow blotches, bounded by the leaf veins, appear on the upper leaf surface, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth on the underside in humid weather. Spots brown and coalesce, and severe infection rapidly defoliates the vines.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread until the leaves die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like water mold that spreads on wind-borne spores and needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect, so it flares in wet, humid spells and dewy conditions. It moves fast once established and is favored by crowding and prolonged leaf wetness.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that spreads in wet, humid weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide, covering leaf undersides, when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet and feeds the infection.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in humid weather, when the disease can appear and spread quickly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, and watch closely in humid weather. Choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole vines, wilt and collapse even though the soil is moist, often spreading until the plant dies. A field test helps confirm it: cut a wilted stem and slowly draw the cut ends apart, and infected sap pulls into thin, sticky white strands.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Vines wilt and die even though the soil is wet. If you cut a wilted stem and pull the two ends apart slowly, infected sap stretches into sticky white strings.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium spread by striped and spotted cucumber beetles, which carry it in their gut and infect plants as they feed. It clogs the water-conducting tissue, so the plant wilts despite adequate water. Pumpkin and squash are generally less susceptible than cucumber and melon, but losses still occur.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ spread by cucumber beetles as they feed. It blocks the plant's water pipes, so the vine wilts even when watered.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants to limit spread. Control is really beetle control, so management aims at keeping cucumber beetle numbers down, especially early in the season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is keeping cucumber beetles down, since they spread it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Manage cucumber beetles from seedling stage with row cover removed at flowering, keep young plants vigorous, and remove infected plants promptly. Controlling the beetle vector is the most effective control of the disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep cucumber beetles under control, since they spread the disease. Cover young plants until they flower, and pull any plant that wilts and tests positive.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, collapsing crowns and a soft, white-mold fruit rot, especially on fruit resting on wet soil, with vines wilting in low, poorly drained spots after heavy rain. It can rot fruit in the field and in storage and persists in the soil for years.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pumpkins resting on wet ground develop a soft, white, moldy rot, and vines collapse in low, soggy spots after heavy rain. It can spread to fruit in storage.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne water mold (Phytophthora) that thrives in saturated soil and standing water, spreading by spores in splashing and running water. Wet, poorly drained ground and fruit in direct contact with soaked soil drive it; the pathogen survives in soil for years.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soilborne disease that loves wet, poorly drained ground and standing water. It spreads in splashing water and rots fruit that sits on wet soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for infected plants; remove and destroy them and affected fruit. Management is cultural: improve drainage, never let water stand, and harvest fruit promptly off wet ground.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, so remove infected plants and rotted fruit. The main thing is to fix drainage and keep water from standing around the plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on raised beds or hills for drainage, avoid low or poorly drained ground, do not overwater, rotate out of cucurbits and other hosts on a long cycle, and lift ripening fruit onto a board or mulch to keep it off wet soil.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant on raised hills so water drains away, avoid soggy spots, and do not overwater. Set ripening pumpkins on a board or thick mulch so they are not sitting on wet ground.
